title: Two Rooms, Same Thursday
sendTrigger: Send this to whoever still has a fridge they are scared to open.
editorialNotes: Only external stat is the EPA April 2025 figure ($2,913, sourced in gtm.json). No user counts or traction claims.
Slide 7 states pre-launch status and says "a TestFlight beta coming this summer"; today is 2026-10-02, so that phrase is stale and the post needs a hold plus Adi review before it ships.

copy.headline: On Thursday nights I push carts at a food pantry. On weekends I serve dinner at a retirement home.
In one room, people need food.
items: In the other, food gets thrown away.
Both rooms are within fifteen minutes of my house.

copy.headline: Nobody in either room is doing anything wrong.
items: The pantry is run by people who show up in the rain.
The kitchen follows food safety rules it has to follow.
The waste is not a villain.

copy.heroNumberCaption: The average American household of four throws away $2,913 of food a year.
copy.body: That is the national version of the thing I was watching happen in one building on one night.

copy.headline: Here is what I kept getting stuck on.
items: There is no moment where someone chooses it.
It happens because the food stops being visible long before it stops being good.

copy.headline: So I built something.
copy.body: I am seventeen, I did not have a formal coding background when I started, and I used AI to close the gap between what I could picture and what I could actually ship.

copy.headline: It is called fond. It is not launched yet.
items: There is a waitlist, a TestFlight beta coming this summer, and no user numbers I can honestly quote you.
I would rather tell you that than inflate it.

copy.headline: I do not think the answer to wasted food is telling people to care more. I think it is making the thing visible while there is still time to act on it.
copy.ctaLine: Building an app that makes what is in your kitchen impossible to forget.
